title: Dreaming — the self creates its own world (4.3)
hook: there are no roads or chariots in a dream, and yet you ride one: who built it?
tomorrow: deep sleep — the embrace of the beloved

segments.voice: Yesterday: jyotis. When the sun, moon, fire and speech are gone, the self is their light. Your line was your own light.

Last night, maybe, you were at a train station you've never seen. Someone who died years ago was there, talking normally. The house you grew up in had an extra room. Nobody built that station, and there's no train in your bedroom. So where did it come from, and what was lighting it, with your eyes closed in a dark room? Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka, turns to the place a sleeper goes at night.
screen: `A STATION YOU'VE NEVER SEEN.` → `NO TRAIN IN YOUR BEDROOM.` → `WHO BUILT IT?`

segments.voice: A person has two places, Yajnavalkya says: this world, and the other world. And there's a third, where the two meet: sleep, dreaming. Standing there, you can see both. When a person dreams, he takes the material of this whole world, tears it down himself, builds it up himself, and dreams by his own brightness, by his own light. There, the person is his own light. Then the passage that gives today its line. There are no chariots there, no horses, no roads. But he makes chariots, horses, roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures, no delights. But he makes joys, pleasures, delights. There are no ponds, no lakes, no rivers. But he makes ponds, lakes, rivers. For he is the maker. Notice two things. First, the building material is borrowed: the station is made out of stations you've seen, the face out of faces you know. Nothing comes from nowhere. Second, the light. Yesterday, the self was the light left when every other light was gone. In the text, a dream is the proof: the room is dark, the eyes are shut, and still everything is lit. People see his playground, the text says, but nobody sees him. And a small, practical line: don't wake a sleeping person suddenly, people say; it's hard to heal someone who doesn't find their way back. Later Hindu schools argued over who really does the building in a dream, the dreamer or God, and what dreams say about waking. The Upanishad leaves it here: the dreamer builds.
screen: `THE THIRD PLACE: WHERE TWO WORLDS MEET.` · `NO CHARIOTS THERE; HE MAKES THEM.` · `BORROWED MATERIAL, HIS OWN LIGHT.` · `THEY SEE HIS PLAYGROUND, NOT HIM.` · then, large: `THE DREAMER BUILDS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and build a place you love, slowly: a beach, a kitchen, a street, the color of the walls, the sound, the smell, all made of things you've seen. Notice that it's lit, though your eyes are closed; then let the picture fade, and stay with the light that was showing it to you.
Dreaming. Where, Yajnavalkya says, the person is svayamjyoti, self-luminous, lit by its own light: no sun, no lamp, and still everything shows.
Your line: the dreamer builds. Tomorrow, one floor deeper, below the dreams. That's day three hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers use the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep, laid out in this part of the Brihadaranyaka and in the Mandukya Upanishad, to point to the self that is present in all three.

fork.setup: in your dream you're riding in a chariot down a long road. but there are no chariots or roads in a dream. where did they come from?
options: you made them, out of this world's material.
fork.reveal: he makes chariots, horses and roads, for he is the maker. the material is borrowed from waking life; the light is his own.

original.note: Sanskrit svayaṃ (by itself) + jyotis (light): self-luminous. atrāyaṃ puruṣaḥ svayaṃjyotiḥ (4.3.9).

trapdoor: what you thought: dreams are random noise.
what it means: in a dream the self builds a world from borrowed material and lights it with its own light.
what a scholar hears: 4.3.9–14 make dream the 'third place' (saṃdhya sthāna) and the proof of svayaṃjyotis; the Brahma Sutras (3.2) later debate who creates dreams.

svayamjyoti.meaning: self-luminous, lit by its own light

Upanishad.meaning: one of the old teaching texts at the end of the Vedas

notes: 4.3.9–10 paraphrased closely: two places plus the third (sandhya), the chariots/joys/ponds triad, 'for he is the maker' (sa hi kartā). Confirm.
'People see his playground; nobody sees him' (ārāmam asya paśyanti, na taṃ paśyati kaścana) and the waking-suddenly line (4.3.14): paraphrased; confirm.
Brahma Sutras 3.2.1–6 cited for the later debate on whether the individual or the Lord creates dream objects; confirm the reference.
The bird verses (4.3.11–13) are omitted for length.
